title: Predictive prefetch + sparse-pin coordinator for paged KV cache
author: Aisha Kumar
description: Context: We observed recurring tail-latency spikes on token generation workloads driven by sporadic cold misses in the paged KV cache. Existing pinning strategies (full-span sticky pins) reduce miss rate but increase memory pressure and harm throughput under mixed workloads. This PR introduces two complementary mechanisms: 1) a lightweight, trainable hotset predictor that drives proactive asynchronous prefetching for likely-needed KV pages, and 2) a sparse-pin coordinator that pins only a sampled subset of page spans based on access probability and epoch stability heuristics. Together these reduce cold-miss latency while keeping resident working set size bounded. Goals: reduce 95/99th token latency for long-chat workloads, keep average token throughput stable under bursty traffic, and avoid regressing memory utilization for multi-tenant Dedicated pools. What changed (high level): - new hotset predictor module (serving/cache/hotset_predictor.{rs,py}): uses an exponential-weighted frequency sketch + tiny exponentially decaying LSTM-lite model (feature-engineered) for per-model hotness score; cold start tuned to avoid aggressive prefetch. - async prefetcher (serving/cache/async_prefetch.{rs}): issues low-priority non-blocking prefetch requests to the block manager; integrates with scheduler to respect latency SLOs and capacity quotas. - sparse-pin coordinator (serving/cache/sparse_pin_coordinator.{rs}): replaces sticky span pins with epoched sparse pins; pins are probabilistic and promoted when repeated hits occur within an epoch. - scheduler hints and kernel integration (serving/runtime/scheduler_hints.{rs}, runtime/kernels/kv_hinting.h): prefetch/pin hints are exposed to the runtime kernel selection layer to prefer lower-latency execution paths for predicted-hot requests. - metrics, tracing, unit and microbench tests (observability/metrics_hotset.md, tests/kv_prefetch_tests/*, bench/continuous_batching_prefetch_bench). Performance summary (benchmarks run on Dedicated dev cluster with A100s): - 95th token latency improved by 18% on long-chat trace (1000-3000 tokens) with mixed concurrency (20-60 clients). - 99th token latency improved by 24% on same trace. - End-to-end tokens/sec unchanged (within +/- 4%) for steady-state high-throughput runs; under bursty tail scenarios throughput improved by up to 10% due to fewer blocking cache fills. - Resident memory usage grew by ~3.2% on average for workloads with high locality; for low-locality workloads sparse-pin coordinator reduced peak resident set by ~6% vs previous sticky pins. Safety and operational controls: - prefetch throttles are on a per-customer quota and global circuit-breaker. - feature is behind a runtime flag (redwood.runtime.features.prefetch_predictor) and rollout controlled via console. - onboarded canary tests in perf-canary repo to exercise bursts and low-locality mixes. Rollout plan: - Step 1: internal canary (10% of Hosted traffic) with aggressive logging for two weeks. - Step 2: Dedicated pools opt-in via console; default off for existing Dedicated customers. - Step 3: gradual ramp to 50% if metrics stable. Motivation and trade-offs: The predictor purposely favors conservative precision to avoid wasteful prefetch; we found that false positive prefetches are cheaper than synchronous blocking misses but only up to a point, hence the sparse-pin approach which narrows what gets pinned. This design reduces tail-latency but requires careful quota management and visibility to customers. Related work: builds on previous allocator improvements (see ENG-4321-style block coalescing), but intentionally orthogonal to the block-pool compaction changes in PRs that focused on defragmentation. See linked Linear tasks for tuning experiments.
